title: Abell 2744 (Hubble)
caption: Abell 2744, or Pandora's Cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: Image: NASA, ESA, HFF Team, Jennifer Lotz (STScI), Matt Mountain (STScI), Anton Koekemoer (STScI)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Many yellow and white galaxies are scattered across black space, the biggest near the center, with thin blue-white streaks and tiny red points sprinkled between them. This is Abell 2744, nicknamed Pandora's Cluster, formed as four smaller galaxy clusters piled together.

The cluster's mass is so great that its gravity bends light from galaxies far behind it, making them look bigger and brighter. This gravitational lensing lets astronomers study early galaxies that would otherwise be too distant to see in detail. Because Abell 2744 has been studied so thoroughly, including by Hubble, researchers can model precisely how the lens distorts background images and then work out how those galaxies would look without it.

When this image was released in 2019, a team headed by Tommaso Treu (University of California, Los Angeles) planned to use the cluster with the James Webb Space Telescope, then slated to launch in March 2021. They hoped to learn whether the first galaxies made the universe transparent to light, and how later galaxies spread heavier elements.
scale: The cluster lies about 3.5 billion light-years away, according to NASA.

understand.summary: A Hubble Space Telescope image. NASA has not published the filters or color mapping for this image.
understand.eye: NASA has not published the color mapping, so the colors should not be taken as what an eye would see, and the lensed background galaxies are too faint and distant for the eye.

explore: After the big bang, the cooling universe filled with neutral hydrogen that blocked light. Scientists think the first galaxies gave off enough ultraviolet light to break up that hydrogen, ending what are called the dark ages. The team also planned deep infrared images of two fields beside the cluster to count galaxies in the very early universe.
